title: Electrophysiological measurements of synaptic connectivity and plasticity in the longitudinal dentate gyrus network from mouse hippocampal slices
protocol: Anaesthetize a 3–4-week-old mouse by isoflurane inhalation in a closed chamber inside a fume hood.
Decapitate the mouse when its breathing slows to around one beat per second.
Isolate the whole brain with dissection tools, being careful not to touch the hippocampus.
Cut the skin from the base of the skull toward the nose using standard scissors.
Peel and cut away the skin on the top and sides to completely expose the skull.
Make lateral cuts on both sides of the vertebrae and cut through the jaw bones.
Insert one blade of the microscissors under the skull and cut towards the eyes along the midline.
At the bregma line, make two lateral cuts on the skull from the midline towards the eyes.
Use forceps to open the skull from the incision and expose the whole brain.
Avoid applying pressure onto the brain while removing the skull.
Insert the thin, flat end of the spatula near the olfactory bulb and scoop up the brain from the ventral side.
Gently cut the optic and cranial nerves with the spatula to free the brain from the skull.
Gently submerge the brain into the 50 mL beaker containing the slicing medium for 20 s on ice.
Dissect out the hippocampus and transfer it to the vibratome.
Transfer the brain onto the cold petri dish.
Use a stainless-steel spoon to transfer the brain, ensuring that only the rostroventral side of the brain comes in contact with the spoon.
Cut out the cerebellum using a scalpel.
Separate the left and right hemispheres with a clean top-down cut using a scalpel.
Insert the blunt end of one spatula into the gap between the cerebral cortex/hippocampus and the midbrain.
Use this to hold down the tissue but avoid pressing the spatula onto the cerebral cortex/hippocampus.
Cut away the midbrain, thalamus, and septum.
Gently isolate the hippocampus from the cerebral cortex using scraping motions with a blunt end.
Cut out the septal and temporal ends of the hippocampus using a scalpel.
Spread a thin layer of superglue on masking tape, covering approximately 3 x 3 mm.
Transfer the hippocampus onto the curved side of the spatula using a fine brush.
Touch the brush on tissue paper to wick away any excess solution from the brain.
Stick the CA3 (rostral) side of the hippocampus on the glue layer.
Submerge the disc inside the buffer tray.
Orient the disc so that the tissue is sliced from the septal to the temporal end rather than from CA1 to DG.
Produce hippocampal slices using a vibratome.
Set the thickness to 300 μm for whole-cell patch recording.
Set the thickness to 400 μm for extracellular field recording.
Cut away the top 500–600 μm of tissue from the animal's brain.
Slice until the CA1 and DG regions are visible under light microscopy.
Gently transfer slices into an inner chamber containing oxygenated ACSF or slicing medium using a blunted disposable pipette.
Keep the slices submerged during the transfer process.
Remove any air bubbles from the inner chamber without touching the slices.
Let the brain slices rest inside the holding chamber, which is continuously oxygenated.
Place the entire holding chamber in a 32°C water bath for whole-cell patch recording for 30 minutes.
Transfer the holding chamber to room temperature after 30 minutes and let it rest for an additional 30 minutes minimum.
Rest brain slices at room temperature for at least one hour if performing extracellular field recordings.
Turn on the electronic equipment and computer software.
Set up the Molecular Devices Axon CNS MultiClamp 700B Microelectrode Amplifier on a vibration-free table.
Set up the Axon Digidata 1550B Data Acquisition System on the same table.
Install and configure Clampex software on the computer.
Mount a Dual-arm micromanipulator on the setup.
Connect and set up Perfusion pumps for use.
Configure a Perfusion temperature controller.
For whole-cell patch recording, mount an Ultima In Vitro Multiphoton Microscope System.
Attach a Bruker Galvanometer Driver to the system.
Install Prairie Technologies Galvanometer Control software.
Launch Prairie View software on the computer.
For extracellular field recording, set up a MASTER-9 Pulse Stimulator.
Connect and configure an ISO-Flex Stimulus Isolator.
Thaw an aliquot of internal solution on ice.
Mount the Current Clamp and Voltage Clamp Headstage on one arm of the micromanipulator.
Attach the silver chloride recording electrode/pipette holder to the setup.
Adjust the angle of the Current Clamp and Voltage Clamp Headstage to 15° from the horizontal plane.
Attach 1 mm diameter tubing to the suction port of the pipette holder.
Attach a 1 mL syringe via a three-way valve to the other end of the tubing.
Insert a silver chloride reference electrode into the bath solution without touching the brain slice.
Ground the reference electrode.
Add picrotoxin to the ACSF perfusion solution (final concentration at 50 μM).
Perfuse the specimen stage with oxygenated ACSF maintained at 31°C–32°C by an automatic temperature controller.
Supply and discharge ACSF at a steady rate (1.5 mL/min) using peristaltic pumps.
Check frequently to ensure that the stage does not flood and there are no excessive vibrations or fluid currents.
Gently transfer one brain slice to the specimen stage with a blunted disposable pipette.
Place a harp on top of the slice to secure its position.
Ensure the laser path reaches the molecular layer of the DG blade without contacting the pipette.
Mind the orientation of the slice so that the laser path does not interfere with the patch process.
Acclimatize the slice on the specimen stage for an additional 30 min.
Visualize one slice with a 10× air objective under bright-field illumination.
Check that the fluid level is stable and there are no vibrations interfering with the patch process.
Switch to a 40× water immersion objective.
Locate the dorsal blade in the DG layer closer to CA1.
Identify healthy DG granule cells by their densely packed, darker-colored soma arrangement under bright-field illumination.
Mark the position of the identified cell with masking tape on the computer monitor.
Add Alexa Fluor 594 to the K-based internal solution (20–50 μM).
Backfill the pulled glass micropipette with the mixed solution.
Aspirate internal solution into a 1 mL syringe.
Attach a 0.2 μm membrane filter to the syringe.
Attach a 70 mm blunt tip microcannula to the filter.
Gently tap the patch pipette to remove any air bubbles from the tip.
Attach the filled micropipette onto the pipette holder, ensuring that the silver chloride wire touches the solution.
Set to voltage-clamp mode [VC] on [MultiClamp 700B commander].
Load the [Membrane Test] function on [Clampex] software and set it to [Bath] mode.
Apply constant positive pressure inside the pipette by injecting a small amount of air with the 1 mL syringe (approximately 0.2 mL).
Position the patch pipette into the bath solution between the objective and the brain slice.
Lift the objective until it just remains in contact with the bath solution.
Do not adjust the X and Y-axis positions of the stage.
Position the patch pipette under the objective so that the shank becomes visible.
Find the tip of the pipette under the microscope.
Lower the patch pipette and objective simultaneously until the pipette tip is just above the target neuron.
With fine control mode of the micromanipulator, position the patch pipette just below the lens until it becomes visible as a shadow under the microscope.
Keep the pipette tip clean by not touching it with anything but the brain slice.
Click [Auto] under [Pipette Offset] on [MultiClamp 700B] software.
Check the tip resistance. The Rt in [Clampex] [Membrane Test], as well as the Resistance in [MultiClamp], should be the same.
Target the tip resistance to be 5–7 MΩ for whole-cell patch recording and 3–4 MΩ for extracellular field recording.
Monitor the waveform of the membrane current and remove electrical noise by monitoring the Scope window (10–20 kHz sampling rate).
Move the patch pipette until the tip becomes clearly visible under the microscope.
Check that the tip is not broken and that there are no debris or air bubbles inside.
Lower the pipette towards the slice while maintaining the tip in focus.
Focus on the target neuron and slowly approach the pipette towards the cell.
Apply gentle suction by pulling out the syringe plunger or via mouth pipetting when the positive pressure inside the pipette produces a slight dent on the cell surface.
Hold the membrane potential at -81 mV in MultiClamp.
Form the seal within approximately 1 min.
Click Cp Fast: [Auto] in MultiClamp to correct for fast capacitance.
Apply more potent suction to rupture the cell membrane.
Optional: Use the Zap function in MultiClamp to deliver a pulse that may help with membrane rupture.
Measure the resting membrane potential (mV) 1 min after applying suction and switching to current-clamp mode [IC].
Configure a two-photon laser microscope equipped with two lasers tuned to excitation wavelengths of 810 nm and 720 nm, respectively.
Switch to a 60× objective lens.
Run a pre-configured protocol in Clampex to inject the threshold current (pA) once every 10 s for 5 min.
Activate Ch1 (Channel 1) button in Prairie View 5.4 software.
Click on Live Scan in Scanning field.
In [Power/Gain] tab, increase the power of the [Imaging] laser by clicking the right arrowhead.
Adjust the PMT intensity until an appropriate amount of brightness is visible in [Image Window].
Define a region of interest around the cell body of the patched neuron and its neurites.
Set [Image resolution] at 512 × 512 with [Average Every] 4 Frames in [Scanning] field.
Optional: Increase [Dwell Time Per Pixel (μs)] to give a clearer image.
Set [Image resolution] at 1024 × 1024 with [Average Every] 2 Frames in [Scanning] field.
Bring the microscope focus to the very top of the neuron.
Click the button to set the [Start Position (μm)].
Bring the focus to the bottom of the neuron.
Click the button to set the stop position (μm).
Stop live scan.
Start Z-series.
Note: Use step size (μm) of 1–2 for good-quality stacked images.
Place the cell body in the middle of the [Image Window].
Record the position P1 = (x1, y1, z1) under [Stage Control].
Adjust the pipette position every 5 minutes to stay close to the cell body.
Prepare 500 μM MNI-caged-L-glutamate in ACSF solution freshly.
Perfuse the prepared solution into the recording chamber.
Wait at least 3 min for the solution to diffuse entirely throughout the recording chamber.
Maintain a stable whole-cell configuration during the entire experiment.
Visualize the unstained brain slice without a halogen light source using Dodt Gradient Contrast (DGC).
Deactivate [Ch1 (Channel 1)] in [Image Window].
Activate [DODT] button.
In [Misc] tab, change [Mirror] to [In] in [Dodt Detector] field.
Click [Live Scan] in [Scanning] field.
Find a target area for photostimulation in the molecular layer (ML) hundreds of microns away from the patched neuron.
Ensure the target area excludes any dendrites extending from the patched neuron.
Optimize laser duration, power, number of stimulation spots, and dot size to elicit an action potential in a neuron.
Start with minimum power (10 mW) for 1 ms laser duration.
Increase parameters incrementally.
Rest slices for 30 seconds between stimulations.
Use a 3 × 3 grid of point stimulation with a laser duration of 5 ms and spot spacing of 10 μm.
Set interpoint delays greater than 0.12 ms.
Adjust the average power to 42 mW, ranging from 7.5 to 78.08 mW.
Ensure the spot size is diffraction-limited between 0.2–1 mm based on laser intensity and objective dependency.
Set [First Repetition] under [Wait for Trigger].
Select [Start with external trigger (Trig 1)] under [Trigger Selection] in Clampex software.
Run the protocol under [IC] mode to record excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs).
Click [Live Scan], then click [Stop Live Scan].
Click [Run Mark Points].
On Clampex, click [Record] and visualize EPSP.
Rest slices for 30 seconds between stimulations.
If an EPSP was evoked, place the stimulation point grid in the middle of [Image Window].
Record the position P2 = (x2, y2, z2) under [Stage Control].
Calculate the distance between the patched neuron and the glutamate uncaging spot.
Add 0.1 mM cadmium chloride (CdCl2) to the perfusate.
Wait a few minutes for CdCl2 to diffuse throughout the recording chamber.
Repeat steps 45–50 at position P2 and record EPSPs under the effect of CdCl2.
Analyze peak amplitudes of all EPSPs offline using Clampfit software.
Secure the concentric bipolar microelectrode connected to the electrical stimulus isolator on one arm of the micromanipulator.
Mount the Current Clamp and Voltage Clamp Headstage (angled at 20°) on the other arm of the micromanipulator.
Backfill the pulled capillary pipette with ACSF and mount it to the recording electrode headstage.
Add picrotoxin to the ACSF perfusion solution to achieve a final concentration of 50 μM.
Perfuse the specimen stage with oxygenated ACSF maintained at 31°C–32°C using peristaltic pumps (flow rate: 1.5 mL/min).
Check frequently for flooding and excessive vibrations or fluid currents on the specimen stage.
Gently transfer one brain slice to the specimen stage using a blunted disposable pipette.
Place a harp on top of the brain slice to secure its position.
Acclimatize the brain slice on the specimen stage for an additional 30 minutes.
Locate the dorsal DG blade under a 10× objective lens.
Load the [Membrane Test] function on Clampex software.
Record the tip resistance as you lower the recording electrode until it touches the solution with the micromanipulator.
Replace the glass tip if the resistance is out of the desired range (3–4 MΩ).
Visualize the signals on the Scope window at a 10–20 kHz sampling rate to check for electrical noise.
Using the micromanipulator, lower the stimulating and recording electrodes to hover just above the slice.
Lower the stimulating electrode to lightly come into contact with the inner molecular layer (IML) of the dorsal blade of DG granule cell layer.
Lower the recording electrode to touch the same IML of the dorsal blade of DG granule cell layer 200–400 μm away from the stimulating electrode.
Evoke local field potentials (LFPs) with a minimum constant current at 100 ms duration.
Repeat evocation of LFPs at 30-s intervals.
Adjust the position of the recording electrode to find the area that gives maximum amplitudes and an exemplary shape of LFPs.
If no responses are detected, change the location of the recording electrode or use another brain slice.
Configure the digitizer, pulse stimulator, and electrical stimulus isolator.
Set the mode on [Master-9 Pulse Stimulator] to TRIG (delivers a single pulse).
Set the duration on [Master-9 Pulse Stimulator] to 100 μs.
Set the number of pulses on [Master-9 Pulse Stimulator] to 1.
Set the voltage level on [Master-9 Pulse Stimulator] to the lowest voltage that can evoke LFPs (e.g., ±3 mV).
Find the lowest intensity in [stimulus isolator] under the [Current (I)] mode.
Increase the intensity amplitude in [stimulus isolator].
Record the peak amplitude of the LFPs at each intensity level (e.g., 0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0).
Ensure a 30-second interval between stimulations to prevent cell damage or changes in short-term synaptic plasticity.
Plot the intensity versus peak amplitude to determine the half-maximum LFP amplitude.
Use this determined intensity for all subsequent stimulation steps.
Evoke and record LFPs every 30 seconds during the baseline recording phase.
Apply a train of tetanus stimuli consisting of four trains at 100 Hz, each lasting 1 second with 1-second intervals between trains to induce long-term potentiation (LTP).
Change back the [Master-9 Pulse Stimulator] settings to those used in the baseline recording after LTP induction.
Evoke and record LFPs every 30 seconds for one hour post-conditioning.
Maintain constant fluid levels and electrode positions throughout the experiment.
